scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In Nago rituals, the standard clay ceremonial cooking pot is replaced by an iron zin, reflecting the dance's deep association with the element of metal and the militant spirit of the Ogou.
This is Nago. 18th-21st century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Nago tradition stems from the Yoruba people brought to Haiti during the Atlantic slave trade.
The term 'Nago' is derived from 'Anagó', a historic exonym for the Yoruba.
The tradition represents a syncretization of Yoruba orisha and rites into the Haitian Vodou framework.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Nago rituals are marked by the call 'Awo che Nago'.
The dance honors the militant, masculine Ogou spirits, who are associated with the elements of earth, fire, and metal.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance features strong thrusting, swaying, shoulder undulations, and pirouettes combined with fast footwork.
It is performed to the rhythm of three Rada cowhide-head drums.
Watch for Shoulder undulations, Strong thrusting.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is provided by three Rada cowhide-head drums.
Rhythmic patterns include the fast-paced Nago Chaud and the slow, heavy Nago Grand Coup.
Listen for the Three Rada cowhide-head drums.
The music is driven by the polyrhythmic interplay of three Rada cowhide-head drums, alternating between fast, driving beats and slow, heavy, percussive pulses.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Nago rites necessitate an iron zin, a ceremonial cooking pot, instead of the typical clay vessel used in other Vodou rituals.
on_screen: Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Loco, known as the 'king of the Nago' (wa Nago), is the leader of the Nago nanchon.
The Ogou are the dominant group of lwa within the nanchon.
Veneration of the Nago as a wholly distinct nation is more typical of Northern Haitian Vodou, whereas in other areas, it is often absorbed into Rada or Petwo rites.
The tradition is a syncretization of Yoruba religion, specifically the orisha, into the Haitian Vodou nanchon system.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Nago is a religious practice within Haitian Vodou; outsiders should observe rituals with respect and follow the guidance of practitioners regarding participation and photography.
